newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma celebrates military day without incident.
newsitem.headline: Burma celebrates military day without incident.

text.p: Burma's military government celebrated its 52nd Armed Forces Day on Thursday amid tight security, with its top general calling on soldiers to be united in destroying "destructive elements".
Despite government fears of trouble, no incidents were reported.

General Than Shwe, chairman of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), warned about 5,000 soldiers in Resistance Park to be wary of traitorous elements who were trying to destabilise the nation.

"You, comrades, must be ever prepared to oppose and crush with revolutionary spirit... instigative acts to perpetrate terrorism and anarchism," he said in a speech that sounded similar to those delivered over the past few years.

"You, comrades, must remember that protecting our country against internal and external destructive elements is our national duty," he told soldiers who assembled in the park after marching past the golden Shwedagon Pagoda.
The soldiers were weighed down by strands of jasmine garlands hung around their necks by people who watched them sing and march through the streets just after dawn.

The government's fear of attacks was apparent on streets near the park and parade route. Over the past few weeks there has been a rapid rise in the number of soldiers at checkpoints and standing guard on streets in the capital.
Sweeps for mines and bombs were done several times a day.
Authorities said the government was worried about possible attacks by ethnic insurgents during Armed Forces Day, when all the top military brass were together in the capital.
There were however no reports of any attacks on Thursday.

Security has also been beefed up because of clashes between Buddhist monks and Moslems. The religious troubles began 12 days ago when monks went on a rampage in Mandalay, setting off attacks on Moslem property and protests by monks across Burma.
Than Shwe did not idetify the "destructive elements" to whcih he referred, but top officials and state media often use the phrase in talking about opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Suu Kyi held a separate celebration at her home to honour people who fought for Burma's struggle for independence.

Suu Kyi, the daughter of independence martyr General Aung San, presented 16 members of her National League for Democracy (NLD) party with certificates to commemorate their role in the independence struggle against Britain.
The 1991 Nobel Peace laureate spoke briefly at the celebration, attended by about 750 people allowed through barricades that have blocked access to her house for months.
"These people fought and won independence," Suu Kyi said. "I believe they will now take part in the democracy revolution. We are waging a democracy revolution as we want to build a nation."

Since her release from six years of house arrest in July 1995, Suu Kyi has made repeated, unanswered requests to the government to hold a dialogue with the opposition to find a way to bring democracy back to Burma.
The NLD won a landslide victory in a 1990 election but the SLORC never accepted the results.
Diplomats saw as significant the fact the SLORC allowed Suu Kyi's celebration to take place at her house, which doubles as the NLD headquarters.
"The fact that it was allowed to go on is a very positive development," one diplomat said. "Although compared to other times, the NLD comment was very restrained."
The NLD has been virtually silent over the past few weeks of religious strife.
